setup_steps.title: Add a stylesheet
setup_steps.body: In the folder with your index.html, add a new file called style.css.

setup_steps.title: Link it to your page
setup_steps.body: Inside the <head> of index.html, add this line: <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">. Save the file.

setup_steps.title: Check that it works
setup_steps.body: In style.css, type h1 { color: red; } and save. Refresh your page. If the heading turns red, the two files are connected.

project_ideas.title: Style your org's page
project_ideas.brief: Take a page you built in HTML and give it a look of its own. Choose colors and fonts that suit it, space things out, and make sure it works on a phone.
done_when: All the styles live in style.css, not in the HTML.
The page uses at most three main colors.
A row of items sits side by side using Flexbox.
The page is easy to read at phone width.

topics.title: Selectors and rules
topics.summary: Write CSS rules that choose elements and change how they look.
topics.why_it_matters: HTML says what things are, but not how they should look. CSS lets you style a whole site from one file.

key_terms.definition: The part of a rule that chooses which elements to style.
One property and its value, like color: red;
A name you give elements so you can style them together.

topics.explanation:
A plain HTML page works, but it looks the same as every other plain page. CSS changes that without touching your content.

A CSS rule has two parts. The selector chooses which elements to style. The declarations, inside curly braces, say what to change. Each declaration is a property, a colon, a value and a semicolon.

A selector can be a tag name like p, which matches every paragraph. To style only some elements, add a class attribute in your HTML, then select it with a dot, like .notice. Keep your rules in a separate style.css file, so one change updates every page.
tips: If nothing changes, check that style.css is linked and that you saved the file before refreshing.
A missing semicolon or curly brace can quietly break the rule after it, so check the line before the problem too.

skill_questions.prompt: Which selector matches elements with class="card"?
In this rule, which part is the selector?

topics.title: Colors and text
topics.summary: Choose colors and fonts that make a page pleasant to read.
topics.why_it_matters: Most of a web page is text. Good colors and fonts decide whether people stay and read or give up.

key_terms.definition: A color written as # and six characters, like #C7366F.
How much text stands out from the background behind it.
The typeface used for text, with backups in case it's missing.

topics.explanation:
You can give colors by name, like tomato, but most sites use hex codes like #C7366F because they can be any exact shade. The color property changes the text. The background-color property changes what's behind it.

For text, font-family picks the typeface. Always list a backup, such as sans-serif, in case the first font isn't available. The font-size property sets how big the text is, font-weight makes it bolder, and text-align moves it left, right or to the center.

Check your contrast. Pale gray on white may look stylish, but many people can't read it. Dark text on a light background is always a safe start.
tips: Set font-family and color on body once. The elements inside it inherit them, so you don't have to repeat them.
Stick to two fonts and a few colors. More than that usually looks messy.

skill_questions.prompt: Which property changes what's behind the text?

choices: It's a backup if Verdana is missing

quiz_items.hint: It's two words joined by a hyphen.

quiz_items.hint: It's two words joined by a hyphen.

quiz_items.hint: CSS uses the American spelling.

quiz_items.prompt: A hex color starts with the character ___
quiz_items.hint: It's the hash sign.

topics.title: The box model
topics.summary: Control the space inside and around elements.
topics.why_it_matters: Crowded pages are hard to read, and most spacing problems come from one idea. Once you see every element as a box, spacing stops being guesswork.

key_terms.definition: Space inside an element, between its content and its border.
The line around an element's padding.
Space outside an element, between it and its neighbors.

topics.explanation:
Every element on a page is a rectangular box, even when you can't see the edges. From the inside out, the box has four layers: the content, the padding, the border and the margin.

Padding adds room inside the box, so text doesn't touch the edge. A background color fills the padding too. Margin pushes other elements away, and it's always see-through.

By default, width only measures the content, so padding and border make the box wider than you asked for. Adding box-sizing: border-box makes width include them, which is much easier to work with. Many developers apply it to everything at the start of their CSS.
tips: Lost? Add border: 1px solid red; to an element for a moment to see exactly where its box is.
Right-click the page and choose Inspect. The browser draws each element's padding, border and margin for you.

skill_questions.prompt: Which property adds space inside an element's border?
With box-sizing: border-box, how wide is this box on the page?

quiz_items.prompt: Add space inside a box: .card { ___: 16px; }
quiz_items.hint: It's the layer between the content and the border.

quiz_items.prompt: Add space outside a box: .card { ___: 16px; }
quiz_items.hint: It's the outermost layer.

quiz_items.prompt: Draw a line around a box: .card { ___: 1px solid black; }
quiz_items.hint: It sits between the padding and the margin.

quiz_items.prompt: Make width include padding: box-sizing: ___;
quiz_items.hint: It has a hyphen and ends in the word box.

topics.title: Layout with Flexbox
topics.summary: Line elements up in rows and columns with Flexbox.
topics.why_it_matters: Elements stack on top of each other by default. Navigation bars and rows of cards need things side by side, and Flexbox makes that simple.

key_terms.definition: The parent element that has display: flex.
A direct child of a flex container.

topics.explanation:
Without help, most elements stack from top to bottom. To put them side by side, add display: flex to their parent. The parent becomes the flex container, and its direct children become flex items in a row.

You control the layout from the container. The gap property adds space between the items. The justify-content property spreads them along the row, with values like center or space-between. The align-items property lines them up across it, so center makes them meet in the middle.

To stack items again, use flex-direction: column. If they run out of room, flex-wrap: wrap lets them continue on a new line, which helps on phones.
topics.example:
One

Two
tips: Put display: flex on the parent, not on the items you want to move.
Only direct children become flex items. Something nested deeper doesn't take part.

skill_questions.prompt: To put three cards side by side, which element gets display: flex?
Which property adds space between flex items?

quiz_items.prompt: Turn on Flexbox: .row { display: ___; }
quiz_items.hint: It's the first part of the word Flexbox.

quiz_items.prompt: Add space between items: .row { ___: 16px; }
quiz_items.hint: It's a short word for an empty space.

quiz_items.prompt: Stack items instead: flex-direction: ___;
quiz_items.hint: The opposite of a row.

quiz_items.prompt: Center items along the row: ___: center;
quiz_items.hint: It starts like the word used for lining up text at both edges.

topics.title: Responsive design
topics.summary: Make a page work well on phones and on big screens.
topics.why_it_matters: Many people will open your site on a phone. A page built only for a laptop becomes tiny or cut off there.

key_terms.definition: Able to change its layout to fit any screen size.
A CSS block that only applies at certain screen sizes.
The visible area of the page in the browser.

topics.explanation:
A fixed layout that fits a laptop won't fit a phone. A responsive page adapts instead, and it takes three steps.

First, add the viewport meta tag to your <head>. Without it, phones shrink the whole page as if it were a desktop site.

Second, avoid fixed widths. Use max-width: 100% on images so they never overflow, and let boxes shrink with the screen.

Third, use a media query when the layout needs to change. The rules inside @media only apply when its condition is true, such as a screen that's 600px wide or less. A common use is switching a row of cards into a single column.
topics.example:
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

<style>
  img {
    max-width: 100%; /* never wider than the screen */
  }

  @media (max-width: 600px) {
    .row {
      flex-direction: column; /* stack on phones */
    }
  }
</style>
tips: Make your browser window narrow as you work. It's the quickest way to see how the page behaves on a phone.
Put media queries after your normal rules. When two rules match, the later one wins.

skill_questions.prompt: When do the rules in this block apply?
Which rule stops an image from overflowing a small screen?

quiz_items.prompt: A media query starts with @___
quiz_items.hint: It's in the name: a ___ query.

quiz_items.prompt: Keep images inside the screen: img { ___: 100%; }
quiz_items.hint: It sets the largest width allowed.

quiz_items.prompt: Tell phones to use their real width: <meta name="___" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
quiz_items.hint: It's the word for the visible area of the page.

quiz_items.prompt: Apply rules on small screens: @media (___: 600px) { }
quiz_items.hint: Rules apply up to this width, and no wider.
